When a strong acid is added to water, several processes occur:

1. The acid molecules dissociate completely into ions
2. These ions become hydrated (surrounded by water molecules)
3. The hydration process releases energy in the form of heat (exothermic)

This is why the standard safety procedure when diluting strong acids is "always add acid to water" (and never water to acid). When done rapidly, the heat generated can be significant enough to cause the solution to boil or splatter, potentially causing chemical burns.

For a non-oxidizing strong acid like hydrochloric acid (HCl) or sulfuric acid (H2SO4), the rapid dissolution in water generates significant heat due to the exothermic nature of the hydration process of the ions.
